title: Hypocrisy of Spiritual Leaders
english: …The Savior criticized the scribes and Pharisees, saying they were hypocrites who focused on minor details of the law, such as tithing the anise and the cumin, while neglecting the more important aspects, like judgment, mercy, and faith (Matthew 23:23).

They were driven by greed and a love of money, which led them to oppress and dominate others, and they would bring lawsuits against those who failed, in order to gain more, and even beyond what they were capable of, they would still try to extract more (Matthew 23:23).

He warned the people that their rulers were taking advantage of them, and that they should not follow their example, saying, 'My people, your rulers oppress you, and those who collect taxes dominate you' (Matthew 23:12, Isaiah 3:12).

The Savior's words were a call to the people to recognize the hypocrisy of their leaders and to seek a more authentic and compassionate way of living, striving to be humane and philanthropic, and to maintain a good relationship with God.
He used the metaphor of threshing floors and grape harvests to illustrate the extent of the rulers' greed and oppression, emphasizing the severity of their actions and the need for change.

But already they are laying hands on and pressuring those who are still left, dominating them with an iron fist, rather than guiding them gently as teachers should, forcing their own thoughts and desires upon their followers, rather than allowing them to grow and learn in a nurturing environment.

But this was not the goal of those who followed Christ, who were called to be examples of the flock, not lording their power over others, as the apostle Peter encouraged those who were called to oversee and guide the flock to do so in a humble and servant-like manner (1 Peter 5:3).

The mystical word, or the deeper spiritual truth, recognizes that there are other forces at work, other practitioners who seek to dominate and control, and it is necessary for those who want to live a life of integrity and righteousness to avoid these influences, for there are evil powers that oppose us, that seek to turn our minds and hearts towards what is vile and corrupt, and they demand from us a kind of tax, a payment in the form of our inclination towards passion and sin.
And indeed the holy one blesses…
translator_notes: The text ends mid-sentence: 'καὶ γοῦν ὁ ἱερὸς μακαρίζει'
The term 'καλαμῶνται' in the second half of the text refers to the practitioners laying hands on or pressuring people, rather than 'flattering'.
The clause 'καὶ τὰ ὑπὲρ δύναμιν ἔσθ' was missing from the previous draft.

title: Spiritual Strength and the Reproach of Childlessness
english: We are saved by the spiritual strength of God, who is over all, and we preserve the radiant beauty of our own nature.
However, if the help is withdrawn, we will be stripped of all good, and having lost the beauty of our virtuous boasts, we will be subject to the passions of dishonor and will serve enemies.

In such a state, seven women will seize one man and say, 'We have eaten our own bread and worn our own clothes; only let your name be called over us, and take away our reproach,' which illustrates the desolation and affliction that will befall the cities of Judah.
For the law given through Moses says to the sons of Israel: 'There will not be a barren or sterile one among you' (Deuteronomy 7:14).

In the last reproaches among the Jews, it was said that a woman who does not bear children is barren, that is, someone who is childless among those who have husbands, and this reproach was immediately brought against them.

The law is spiritual, for the God of all things promised that the intellectual Israel, that is, the mind that sees God, will not be unfruitful or sterile, but rather fruitful and a good and excellent land.

It will be, he says, such a scarcity of men in the land, with the war having consumed the race, that seven women will take hold of one man and say, 'We have eaten our own bread and worn our own clothes; only let your name be called over us, and take away our reproach,' demonstrating that they bind their reproach to childlessness and reject the name of the barren and childless.

For they do not come seeking the usual things, nor what it is customary for women to receive from their husbands; for they say they will be sufficient to themselves, and they ask only for the removal of their reproach.

If the one being called upon were rich, the women would not say, 'We have eaten our own bread and worn our own clothes,' because they know that those who have survived the war and escaped are left in extreme poverty and distress.
The women's request is solely for the removal of their reproach, as they are sufficient to themselves and do not require the usual provisions from their husbands.
All your strong men will fall by the sword (Isaiah 3:25).
The text breaks off mid-sentence, ending with 'carrying off the preceding…'
translator_notes: The final clause appears to be an edge fragment; the text breaks off mid-sentence, so it is rendered literally with a trailing ellipsis and noted as uncertain.
The phrase 'in the last reproaches' refers to the final reproaches or insults mentioned in the context of Jewish social customs.

title: Spiritual Abandonment
english: The Israelites have been completed without holy prophets.
At various times, they were taken captive and forced to flee to the lands of the Persians and Medes, accompanied by their wives and loved ones.
However, when they went down to Egypt, they were not without the prophetic guidance of Jeremiah, who served them with words from God, after the Babylonians had taken Jerusalem.
Since they have been persuaded to Christ, they have been abandoned and their security has been shattered, which, I believe, is what is meant by the statement that their wall has been torn down.
The prophetic voice that once guided them has fallen silent, and the word of the holy prophets has ceased to be spoken.

I think this is what God meant when He said, 'Behold, days are coming when I will bring a famine upon the land, not a famine of bread or thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord' (Amos 8:11-12).
They will run from east to west seeking the word of the Lord, but they will not find it.

This has happened to them, and it is only fitting, for they rejected the Lord of powers, who nourishes souls and hearts with spiritual showers, as the psalmist David remembered, saying, 'Like the dew of Hermon coming down upon the mountains of Zion' (Psalm 133:3).

But a new vineyard has been raised up, one that consists of those who have been called to sanctification through faith, and the Bridegroom from heaven, Christ, says of them, 'The vines are in bloom, they have given fragrance'.
Christ himself is the all-holy, the true vine, and we have been separated from him like branches, being filled with his life-giving nourishment.

He clearly says, 'I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer' (John 15:1), and every branch in him that does not bear fruit, he removes, and every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, so that it may bear more fruit.
Since we have been grafted to him through intimacy, it is clear that we have become fruitful, and he teaches us to remain in him, saying, 'Remain in me, and I in you' (John 15:4).

Just as the branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can we unless we remain in him, and he says, 'I am the vine, you are the branches' (John 15:5), and the one remaining in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, because apart from him, we can do nothing.

Therefore, it is necessary to be grafted to the true vine, that is, Christ, through faith and love and obedience to everything, and he himself will declare us fruitful, and he will put a fence around us, and raise up the wall, and separate us.
